d.title: Data drift and concept drift need different monitors
d.caption: Data drift is P(X) moving: the inputs changed. Concept drift is P(Y|X) moving: the **relationship** changed. A model can be perfectly right under data drift and perfectly wrong under concept drift with inputs that look identical — which is why the second monitor needs labels, and therefore always arrives late.

d.title: Three answers to 'what is the parameter', on three heads out of three
d.caption: The MLE says the coin always lands heads, which is the honest maximum of the likelihood and a useless forecast. MAP adds a prior and returns a single number; the posterior returns the **distribution**, and everything else in this lesson is a consequence of carrying it instead of collapsing it.

d.title: Why the posterior makes a good policy
d.caption: Thompson sampling needs no exploration parameter at all: drawing one sample per arm from each posterior and playing the best explores exactly in proportion to how uncertain the arm is, and that proportion shrinks on its own as evidence arrives.

cells.text: acting randomly epsilon of the time

d.title: Prequential evaluation: test on each row before training on it
d.caption: There is no held-out set on a stream, so the honest protocol is to predict each arriving row, record the error, and *then* learn from it. Every row is therefore a test row exactly once, and the running error is an unbiased picture of how the model behaved as the data arrived.

d.title: Non-IID is not one problem
d.caption: Federated averaging degrades for different reasons depending on **how** the clients differ, and the fix differs with it. Label skew is the one that breaks naive averaging hardest: each client's update points at its own label distribution, and the average of those directions need not help anyone.
cells: personalisation: one model cannot fit all

d.title: Six recommender families, and what each cannot do
d.caption: The failure column drives almost every architecture decision. Collaborative filtering of any kind cannot serve a brand-new item, which is why hybrids exist — not for accuracy, but because the cold start is a certainty rather than a risk.

d.title: The feedback loop, and why offline ranking metrics flatter the old system
d.caption: Held-out clicks were generated by **what the old system chose to show**. A model that reproduces those choices scores well; a model that would have surfaced something better scores badly, because the user never had the chance to click it. Popularity bias compounds it, which is why popularity is a strong offline baseline and a weak product.

d.title: Tokens, stems and lemmas
d.caption: Stemming chops suffixes by rule, so it is fast and produces non-words; lemmatisation looks the word up and needs its part of speech to be right. For a linear model on TF-IDF the difference is usually worth less than the time it costs — which is the finding worth having before reaching for a transformer.

d.title: Cosine on TF-IDF, and what BM25 adds
d.caption: Both rank documents by weighted term overlap. BM25 adds two things TF-IDF lacks: a **saturating** term frequency, so the tenth occurrence of a word adds almost nothing, and an explicit length normalisation with a tunable strength rather than the implicit one that L2 gives.

d.title: Backpropagation is the chain rule, applied in reverse order
d.caption: There is nothing in it beyond the chain rule — the insight is only that computing the derivatives from the output backwards reuses every partial result, so the whole gradient costs about one forward pass rather than one per parameter.

d.title: When a network beats gradient boosting on a table
d.caption: Rarely, and for specific reasons. On a small heterogeneous table boosting wins and a regularised linear model is the yardstick — as this course's churn data showed. A network earns its place when there is a representation to **learn** or to share, which a boosted tree cannot do at all.

d.title: The fairness criteria are mutually incompatible, provably
d.caption: When the base rates differ between groups, equal TPR and equal PPV cannot both hold — that is an impossibility theorem, not a tuning problem. So a team must state which criterion it is claiming and accept the consequence named in the last column. Dropping the protected attribute does not help: it is reconstructable from the other columns.

d.title: A confounder and a collider need opposite treatment
d.caption: This is the asymmetry that makes 'control for everything' wrong. Adjusting for a confounder removes bias; adjusting for a collider **creates** it. No amount of data distinguishes them — only a causal diagram does, which is why the diagram comes before the regression.
